rationale:
I'm going with the radar's fast-turn pick for the long video: Foundayo (orforglipron) and sleep apnea, from the ATTAIN-OSA randomized trials. It's the EloraTZP pattern the playbook backs: a searched drug name, low competition, and the old Foundayo video already draws "foundayo" and "orforglipron" searches. It also clears the fact-check bar because the body rests on the peer-reviewed JAMA paper and the US label, not press releases. The news is only the hook, and the video gets a strong next-step link to Foundayo What to Expect (ssb7Zcs3KSY).

On the search-demand count: 3 of the last 7 long videos already used those formats (SURPASS-CVOT head-to-head, After 6 Months timeline, Vial vs Pen). So today didn't have to be one.

Not re-planned, on purpose:
- Every other queue item is already live (Foundayo What to Expect, Mounjaro vs Ozempic), made (Vial vs Pen) or held for fixes only (Serious Risks, After 6 Months).
- If L1 is held, the publisher should ship the fixed After 6 Months or Serious Risks re-render the same day, before both expire on 11-30.

The Shorts:
- S1 is the required spin-off of L1. It's a practical moment, not a study: "sleeping better, but don't drop your CPAP".
- S2 is a Foundayo practical searched question (holiday drinks), our second-proven Shorts format.
- S3 uses the last day of the holiday 20:00 slot for a day-after felt symptom (queasy the morning after) that our recent holiday Shorts haven't covered.

That makes 2 of the 3 Shorts felt or practical moments, every title puts the drug first, and none repeats a recent angle (bloating, vomiting, constipation, diarrhea, full-the-morning-after and heartburn are all taken).

The carousel reuses the verified 11-20 bruise Short's text as a TikTok photo post, since pen and body moments do best there.

Body systems are spread out: sleep and airway twice, GI once, skin once, plus a drinks or lifestyle piece. No pillar is used more than twice.

pieces.topic: Foundayo (orforglipron) and obstructive sleep apnea: what the ATTAIN-OSA randomized trials showed at 52 weeks, what AHI measures, why weight is linked to sleep apnea, and why it isn't an approved use yet (Zepbound is the GLP-1-based medicine already approved for OSA)
pieces.angle: Keep the structure, but fix the second payoff. Use the JAMA primary results (treatment-regimen estimand). Trial 1, no PAP: average AHI change about −18 events an hour on orforglipron vs about −4.5 on placebo. Trial 2, using PAP: about −17 vs about −5. Card: 'Adults with moderate to severe OSA and a BMI of 27 or more · 52 weeks · orforglipron (highest dose each person tolerated) vs placebo'. Use percentage reductions, remission-or-mild figures and weight change only if the full paper prints them, with the paper's definition and estimand. Otherwise drop them. Chapter 5: 'Lilly said on 9 November 2026 that it plans to ask the FDA to approve it for sleep apnea. Asking for approval isn't approval.' Call trial figures 'adverse events', for example 'gastrointestinal adverse events: 68% vs 37% on placebo in the trial without PAP'. Keep the CPAP don't-stop line, the prescriber line and the watch-next target (ssb7Zcs3KSY).
pieces.working_title: Foundayo (Orforglipron) for Sleep Apnea: What Did the Trial Show?
pieces.why: Exp I fast-turn: a peer-reviewed phase 3 RCT for a drug people search by name, with low creator competition (the EloraTZP pattern), and it feeds the Foundayo What to Expect video. | fact-check: The topic checks out. The JAMA paper exists: Malhotra et al., ATTAIN-OSA, 'Orforglipron for Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Results From 2 Randomized Clinical Trials', published online 9 Nov 2026 (jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2856406). It reports two 52-week phase 3 double-blind trials in adults with moderate to severe OSA and a BMI of 27 or more. Trial 1 had 363 people not using PAP. Trial 2 had 349 people using PAP. Lilly's press release of 9 Nov 2026 says it plans to submit to the FDA by the end of 2026, so the drug is not approved for OSA. One instruction in the angle is wrong. It says to avoid 'the 17–18 figure from the press', but −17.8 and −17.3 events/h are the JAMA paper's own primary results (treatment-regimen estimand). Trial 1: orforglipron −17.8 vs placebo −4.5 (difference −13.2). Trial 2: −17.3 vs −5.3 (difference −12.0). The 43.8%, −21.1 events/h and 31.5% remission-or-mild figures come from Lilly or a different estimand. Use them only if they are in the paper, and name the estimand. The abstract does not give weight change or say how AHI was measured in the PAP trial. Get both from the full text, or leave them out. GI adverse events in the abstract: 68.0% vs 37.4% (Trial 1) and 70.6% vs 36.6% (Trial 2). Call them 'gastrointestinal adverse events'. Name the arm 'orforglipron at the highest dose each person tolerated'. Don't list mg values or anything that reads like a dosing ladder. Population: 'obesity or overweight' (BMI 27 or more), not 'obesity' only. Zepbound's OSA approval covers adults with obesity. Keep it to one neutral line with no comparison. The Foundayo Medication Guide (Revised: 7/2026) pancreatitis wording is confirmed: 'severe pain in your stomach area (abdomen) that will not go away, with or without nausea or vomiting'.

pieces.topic: Sleeping better or snoring less on Foundayo (orforglipron)? Why you shouldn't drop your CPAP on your own
pieces.angle: Hook (14 words or fewer): 'On Foundayo and using CPAP? Keep it until your sleep clinician says otherwise.' Relief fact: 'In two 52-week trials, orforglipron cut breathing interruptions more than placebo did.' Next sentence: 'about 13 fewer an hour than placebo in the trial without CPAP.' Card: 'Adults with moderate to severe sleep apnea, BMI 27+ · one trial with PAP, one without'. Then 'It isn't approved for sleep apnea.', 'If you use CPAP, don't stop or change it on your own.', 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.' and the loop line. Don't say snoring less or sleeping better, and don't name a drug as a CPAP replacement. Watch-next goes to L1 once it's live, otherwise ssb7Zcs3KSY.
pieces.working_title: Foundayo (Orforglipron): Sleeping Better? Keep the CPAP #shorts
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1: a practical moment tied to a searched drug name that sends viewers to the long video. | fact-check: This is a safe and useful angle: it tells viewers not to drop prescribed CPAP. The working title 'Sleeping Better?' could suggest the trial measured how people felt or how much they snored. The primary result was AHI, so stay with breathing interruptions and don't claim less snoring or better sleep. Use L1's verified JAMA figures. The cleanest single number is the placebo-adjusted difference: about 13 fewer events an hour in the trial without PAP and about 12 in the trial with PAP, one number per sentence. Population: adults with moderate to severe OSA and a BMI of 27 or more. It is not approved for OSA. This Short depends on L1's verified figures, so wait for L1's content check.

pieces.topic: Holiday drinks on Foundayo (orforglipron): what the US label covers, and why fluids and pacing matter
pieces.angle: Sentence 1: 'Holiday drinks on Foundayo? Here's what the label does and doesn't say.' Then: 'The Foundayo label doesn't specifically address alcohol.' 'Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea are common.' 'The label says losing fluids from them may cause kidney problems.' Caveat: 'Your risk of low blood sugar may be higher if you also use insulin or a sulfonylurea.' Two untagged tips: 'Sip water alongside, unless you've been told to limit fluids.' 'Skipping the drink is fine too.' Then 'We can't give you a safe amount, so ask your prescriber.', the Foundayo emergency card ('severe pain in your stomach area (abdomen) that will not go away, with or without nausea or vomiting … right away'), the fixed don't-stop line, 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.' and the loop. Watch-next: ssb7Zcs3KSY.
pieces.working_title: Foundayo (Orforglipron) and Holiday Drinks: What the Label Says #shorts
pieces.why: Foundayo paired with a practical searched question is our second-proven Shorts format (food rules 1,062, nausea 853), and holiday parties are starting. | fact-check: Confirmed in the Foundayo PI and Medication Guide at uspl.lilly.com/foundayo/foundayo.html (Revised: 7/2026): neither mentions alcohol, so 'the Foundayo label doesn't specifically address alcohol' is fine. Re-check the full PDF before scripting. Confirmed Medication Guide wording: 'Diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting may cause a loss of fluids (dehydration) which may cause kidney problems.' The angle's caveat is too strong. The guide says low blood sugar risk 'may be higher if you use FOUNDAYO with medicines that can cause low blood sugar, such as an insulin or sulfonylurea', not 'is higher'. Don't claim that alcohol interacts with Foundayo or raises pancreatitis risk, because the label doesn't say so. Don't suggest any 'safe' number of drinks. The holiday is the setting, not the cause.

pieces.topic: Queasy the morning after Thanksgiving dinner on tirzepatide: is that normal, and when to call
pieces.angle: Sentence 1: 'Queasy the day after Thanksgiving on tirzepatide? Nausea is a common side effect on its label.' Card by 6 s: 'Nausea: 28% on top dose vs 8% placebo · adults with obesity or overweight, with or without type 2 diabetes · Zepbound label pool, up to 72 weeks · adverse reactions'. Then the exact escalation sentence. Separate sentence: 'Tirzepatide also slows how fast your stomach empties.' Tips, with no guilt and no making up for the meal: 'Small, bland portions when hunger returns.' 'Sip fluids, unless you've been told to limit fluids.' Then 'Contact your prescriber if you can't keep fluids down.', the tirzepatide emergency card ('with or without vomiting … right away'), the fixed don't-stop line, 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.' and the loop line. Don't use 'mostly'. Leave out the 53% figure.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide: Queasy the Morning After Thanksgiving? #shorts
pieces.why: Last day of the holiday slot. Day-after felt-symptom Shorts are proven (full the morning after 497, stomach pain 271), and day-after nausea hasn't been covered yet. | fact-check: Confirmed in the Zepbound PI at uspl.lilly.com/zepbound/zepbound.html. The sentence 'The majority of nausea, vomiting, and/or diarrhea events occurred during dose escalation and decreased over time.' is real. Table 2 is the pool of Study 1 and Study 2 in adults with obesity or overweight, with or without type 2 diabetes. Nausea: 28% at 15 mg vs 8% on placebo (29% at 10 mg, so call 15 mg 'the top dose' and don't call it 'the highest rate'). Those are label adverse-reaction figures, so the card says 'adverse reactions'. Date conflict: that page prints 'Revised: 8/2026', but the craft notes give Zepbound DailyMed as 16 Nov 2026. Cite the date of the exact document you link. Two framing risks. First, Thanksgiving is the setting: don't say the meal caused the nausea. Second, write 'tirzepatide delays gastric emptying' as its own sentence and don't present it as the cause. Table 2 comes from Zepbound's weight trials, so name that scope on the card. Today is the slot's last day (Thanksgiving was 26 Nov), so it must ship tonight or be dropped.

pieces.why: Pen and body moments are our best format on TikTok (pen blood 1,682), and reusing verified text keeps the carousel safe and cheap to make. | fact-check: Usable only if the 11-20 bruise Short is confirmed as having passed content check. The craft notes list a C1 11-20 that was held for sources, so confirm this isn't the same unverified text. If it is, drop it. Confirmed in the Zepbound PI section 6.1 footnote: the injection-site reaction group 'Includes multiple related adverse event terms, such as injection site bruising, injection site erythema…'. That means 6–8% vs about 2% is the rate for the whole group, not for bruising alone, and the slide must say so. The PI's dosing section also says 'Rotate injection sites with each dose.'
